Area.evidence_source: The positive portrayal of L/G/B people and issues in mass media may help reduce feelings of invisibility, alienation and social isolation for L/B/G youth. Positive representations in the mass media were well known to Zac, who upon realising he was gay, reported being quite elated at the prospect of being able to be part of the "bisexual chic" noveau that was highly regarded in fashion magazines of the time. Positive media images of L/B/G people may be particularly important for young gay and bisexual men who do not know anyone who openly identifies as L/B/G. Commenting on a "gay hour" provided by student radio, Tim illustrates that such programmes can not only directly help reduce a sense of isolation and alienation, but can also inform L/B/G youth about support organisations: . . . So I definitely knew that there were things out there which would provide opportunities, it wasn't like I felt like, you know, there's no where to go now and I'm all stuck by myself. (Tim, 20, non-attempter) Carl emphasised how positive mass media portrayal (in the form of the locally produced Queer Nation television programme) may be an even more vital information source for rural-based youth who otherwise receive little positive information about L/B/G sexualities and possible support groups. Sam also found that positive mass media representations were beneficial during coming-out, because they directly tackled the negative stereotypes that he had of L/B/G people: Ian Roberts was good, because I can remember looking at him, and you know growing up gay you have a negative view of what a gay man is, even from when I was quite young I sort of had this vision of this old man, like an effeminate old man in a room alone with a suitcase and stuff (laugh) this was my vision of what a gay man was. But Ian Roberts being quite a masculine, league player figure, he was quite important just for breaking stereotypes. (Sam, 19, non-attempter) The influence of positive representations in the media was also high-lighted by Leon who commented that the positive portrayal of two gay characters on the national television soap opera Shortland Street were pivotal for him. As mass media both mirrors dominant societal ideologies and cultivates common values and outlooks (Gross, 1991), positive media images may also play a vital role in the formation of more general positive societal attitudes towards L/B/G people. These attitudes may in turn help create an environment more accepting to L/B/G young men who are in the process of coming out. Many L/B/G young people may also find positive role models in people that are part of their everyday lives. Tim detailed how his straight brother's friendship with an openly gay man helped reduce his own feelings of social isolation and how important it was to be shown the possibility of a gay man living a happy, fulfilling life: ... I knew there were stable gay people out there who lead full on lifestyles, and that they could be out and happy, and live like that and not be closeted. ... like it provides you with an option, and, and um, a role model that you know, that there is something out there that you can live that lifestyle. ... (Tim, 20, non-attempter) Carl's testimony impresses how necessary role models of the same ethnicity can be to L/B/G youth. Such role models may provide points to identify with that are consistent with their cultural identities as well as their L/B/G identities: Irirangi Teakiawa, he's like a really awesome, he was like the best, the bombest, um Taiaha, he was really really awesome . . . he's like, the man at doing Taiaha, and Patu and everything, and that he wasn't quite straight, so he was a really big role model. . . . And because he's kind of like, he's kind of in my tribe kind of thing, he definitely is a big idle of mine, . . . especially being Maori. He's Maori, and he was queer, and he was the bomb at doing this and I really appreciate that he came-out just before he died. (Carl, 18, attempter) For L/B/G members of nondominant ethinic groups, who often face the dual discrimination of racism and heterosexism (Erwin, 1993; Savin-Williams & Rodriguez, 1993; Schneider et al., 1989), such role models may be invaluable in proving one can be both "queer" and Maori.
